Situation1: They join in when the family talks about possible weekend plans.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I sat at the kitchen table, my brother’s laughter echoing as my parents tossed out ideas for our weekend together—maybe a hike, maybe a movie night. I smiled, feeling the warmth of belonging, knowing how much it meant to them that I was present, really present, for these moments. My phone buzzed, and I glanced down. A message from the advocacy group: an urgent incident of discrimination had just occurred in our city, and they needed someone to draft a statement and rally support online—immediately. My heart pounded. I knew how important it was to respond quickly, to give voice to those who were silenced, to stand up for what I believed in. But my family was looking at me, waiting for my input, expecting me to be there, to be the sister who cared enough to join in. I felt the weight of both worlds pressing in, the demands of loyalty and love on one side, the call to justice and action on the other. My hands trembled as I tried to decide which part of myself I could let down.
